name: Inuktitut, Eastern Canadian (Latin script)
notes: CODE NOTE: this file is keyed `iu-Latn` (BCP-47 macrolanguage tag + Latn script subtag) rather than the ISO 639-3 individual code `ike`, which is recorded in `iso639_3` below. `ike` is reserved for a future engine fix: the registry's langcodes-based resolver unconditionally canonicalizes individual codes that belong to a macrolanguage into the macrolanguage's own primary tag (`ike` -> `iu`) before checking whether a spec file for `ike` itself exists, the same class of collision documented for `bxr`/`diq` in registry.py's alias table — fixing it for `ike`/`ikt` needs an engine-side alias-table entry, which is out of scope for a data-only change. Eastern Canadian Inuktitut (ᐃᓄᒃᑎᑐᑦ), an Eskimo-Aleut language, a child variety of the Inuktitut macrolanguage (iu). Eastern Canadian Inuktitut is written both in Inuktitut syllabics (qaniujaaqpait — see the `iu` spec, which covers the syllabics tradition in full) and in a Latin romanization (qaliujaaqpait). This file uses the LATIN romanization as primary because a complete, cited letter-by-letter Latin inventory was available (ITK's Inuktut Qaliujaaqpait unified writing system and the Tusaalanga roman-orthography reference), whereas the syllabics side is already covered by the parent `iu` spec and this file does not duplicate it. Phonology mirrors iu: three vowels /i u a/ each with a long counterpart (doubled letter); consonants p t k q ɡ v l j(=/j/) m n ŋ(⟨ng⟩) ʁ(⟨r⟩, uvular) s h, with the geminate velar nasal written ⟨nng⟩ /ŋː/. ⟨ł⟩ /ɬ/ and ⟨h⟩ /h/ are dialect-restricted (present in some Nunavik/Nunavut communities, absent in others), matching the dialect-restricted rows already noted in the `iu` syllabics spec. ⟨g⟩ alternates [ɡ]~[ɣ] the same way the corresponding syllabic glyphs do in `iu`. Consonant gemination beyond ⟨nng⟩ (e.g. doubled ⟨pp⟩, ⟨tt⟩, ⟨kk⟩) is a productive orthographic doubling process, not enumerated here key-by-key; it is not currently representable without a general gemination rule in the engine.
